body_ar:
إن الناس ألفوا أن يقولوا أضمن على الله لك كذا، فهل هذه العبارة مستساغة شرعا؟

أن هذه العبارة مبناها في الأصل على حديث موضوع وقد جاء فيه: «البخيل من لا يضمن على الله» لكن هذا لا يصح عن النبي (ص)، وهو من الموضوعات، فلذلك لا ينبغي أن يقولها الإنسان إلا إذا كان المقصود عنده أن صاحب الفعل إن فعل ذلك ابتغاء مرضاة الله فقد وعده الله خيرا على ذلك الفعل، فهذا القصد، فإنك تستطيع ضمان ما ضمنه الله في كتابه، كل ما تعهد الله به في كتابه أو تعهد به رسوله (ص) فأنت تعلم أنه سيقع فيمكن أن تضمن وقوعه.
body_en:
People have grown accustomed to saying, 'I guarantee upon God that you will have such-and-such.' Is this expression acceptable in the revealed law?

This expression rests, in origin, upon a fabricated hadith (mawḍūʿ), in which it comes: 'The miser is the one who does not guarantee upon God.' But this is not sound from the Prophet, upon whom be peace; it is among the fabrications. For that reason a person should not say it — unless what he means by it is that the one who does the deed, if he does it seeking God's good pleasure, has been promised good by God for that deed. That is the intention that would make it acceptable; for you are able to guarantee what God has guaranteed in His Book. Everything that God has undertaken in His Book, or that His Messenger, upon whom be peace, has undertaken, you know will come to pass — so you can guarantee that it will occur.

flags.context: إن الناس ألفوا أن يقولوا أضمن على الله لك كذا
options: I guarantee upon God that you will have such-and-such
I stand surety with God that you will have such-and-such
I vouch for it with God that you will have such-and-such
flags.note: The whole fatwa turns on the preposition: ضمن على الله is to make oneself guarantor of something AGAINST God, as a debt is guaranteed against a debtor — which is precisely what makes the phrase objectionable, and why the Sheikh permits it only where it means guaranteeing what God has already undertaken in His own Book. A smoother English idiom such as 'I promise you in God's name' would lose the surety relation the answer depends on. The literal rendering has been kept for that reason.

flags.arabic: البخيل من لا يضمن على الله
flags.context: مبناها في الأصل على حديث موضوع وقد جاء فيه: «البخيل من لا يضمن على الله»
options: The miser is the one who does not guarantee upon God
The miser is the one who will not stand surety with God
The niggardly man is he who does not vouch for God
flags.note: The wording is quoted only in order to be rejected: the Sheikh grades it fabricated (mawḍūʿ) and says explicitly that it is not sound from the Prophet. Any display of this article must keep the grading attached to the quotation, since the sentence is quotable on its own and would circulate as a hadith. The Sheikh names no collection and no one who fabricated it.

translator_notes: Hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.
The Sheikh's grading has been carried exactly: the report is fabricated and not soundly established from the Prophet. Nothing has been added and nothing softened.

His ruling on the expression is لا ينبغي, 'should not', with a stated exception — not ḥarām and not makrūh. No ruling word has been supplied for him, and the exception has not been dropped: on his account the phrase is acceptable where the speaker means only to guarantee what God has already undertaken in His Book.
The question is put by the questioner about common usage ('people have grown accustomed'), and the answer is about the phrase, not about any individual.
